```{ojs}
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .5s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1),opacity .4s ease,margin-top .3s ease;margin-top:0;text-align:left;">
      <button class="close-btn" style="display:block;margin:0 auto 10px auto;background:rgba(57,73,171,.15);color:#3949ab;border:none;padding:5px 18px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.85em;min-height:36px;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;">Hide Quiz</button>
      <p style="text-align:center;opacity:.8;font-style:italic;font-size:.9em;margin-bottom:12px;">Select an answer for each question.</p>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  const closeBtn = body.querySelector(".close-btn");
  function expand(){ body.style.maxHeight="5000px";body.style.opacity="1";body.style.marginTop="14px";chevron.style.transform="rotate(180deg)"; }
  function collapse(){ body.style.maxHeight="0";body.style.opacity="0";body.style.marginTop="0";chevron.style.transform="rotate(0)"; }
  toggle.onclick = () => body.style.maxHeight === "0px" || body.style.maxHeight === "" ? expand() : collapse();
  closeBtn.onclick = collapse;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.className = "sp-opt";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        const all = card.querySelectorAll("button.sp-opt");
        all.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";
          all[qq.correct].style.borderColor="#48bb78";
          all[qq.correct].style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    fb.className = "sp-fb";
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  return outer;
}
```

# Engage: What Explains the Patterns in Storm Paths? {#sp-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🗺️ The Investigative Phenomenon

**Maps from 2018–2020 show that blizzards and hurricanes exhibit clear patterns in where they start and the direction in which they travel.**

- **Winter storms** (blizzards) start in the western and central US and sweep **west to east**, curving toward the **northeast**. Many end up over the Northeast and New York City.
- **Atlantic hurricanes** start over the warm **tropical Atlantic**, move **west**, then **curve north and northeast**, sometimes up the East Coast.
- Where storms land has a big impact on how much damage they do, and storm paths **may change as global temperatures rise**.

**Questions for this chapter:** Why do so many winter storms form over the US? What steers storms along these paths? Could warming move the paths, and would NYC get more or fewer winter storms?
:::

Look back at the storm maps from the [Unit Opening](unit5-opening.qmd) (the 2018–19 and 2019–20 winter storm seasons and the 2018 and 2020 Atlantic hurricane seasons). Then think about what you learned in [Blizzards](unit5-blizzards.qmd) about how winter storms form.

# Explore 1: Air Masses Investigation {#sp-explore1}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🌡️ What Is the Air Like Around the World?

Many of you said storms form where **warm, moist** air meets **cold, dry** air. To test that, first find out **where** warm and cold air comes from. You'll look at a world temperature map and a model of how sunlight hits Earth.
:::

## How does energy received from the Sun vary on Earth? {#sp-energy-sun}

In class you use a simulator called **Explore the Effect of the Angle of Incidence on Sun's Energy**. The model below works the same way: a beam of sunlight of the **same width** (same energy) hits Earth at different latitudes. Watch how much ground the beam has to cover.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spMonth = Inputs.radio(["March", "June", "September", "December"], {label: "Select month:", value: "March"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spLoc = Inputs.select(["North Pole", "Tropic of Cancer", "Equator", "Tropic of Capricorn", "South Pole", "New York City"], {label: "Aim the beam at:", value: "Equator"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spLocLat = ({"North Pole": 90, "Tropic of Cancer": 23.44, "Equator": 0, "Tropic of Capricorn": -23.44, "South Pole": -90, "New York City": 40.7})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spDecl = ({"March": 0, "June": 23.44, "September": 0, "December": -23.44})[spMonth]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spEnergy = (lat, decl) => Math.max(0, Math.round(1361 * Math.cos((lat - decl) * Math.PI / 180)))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 560), H = Math.round(W * 0.72);
  const R = H * 0.40, cx = W * 0.62, cy = H / 2;
  const rad = Math.PI / 180;
  const pt = (angDeg) => [cx - R * Math.cos(angDeg * rad), cy - R * Math.sin(angDeg * rad)];
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Side view of Earth lit from the left, with a sunlight beam hitting the chosen latitude");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1324");
  // night side shading
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#1565c0");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", `M ${cx} ${cy - R} A ${R} ${R} 0 0 1 ${cx} ${cy + R} Z`).attr("fill", "rgba(0,0,0,0.45)");
  // latitude lines
  const lats = [90, 66.56, 40.7, 23.44, 0, -23.44, -66.56, -90];
  [66.56, 23.44, 0, -23.44, -66.56].forEach(phi => {
    const a = pt(phi - spDecl), b = pt(180 - phi - spDecl);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", a[0]).attr("y1", a[1]).attr("x2", b[0]).attr("y2", b[1])
      .attr("stroke", phi === 0 ? "#fde68a" : "rgba(255,255,255,0.45)").attr("stroke-width", phi === 0 ? 1.6 : 1).attr("stroke-dasharray", phi === 0 ? null : "4,3");
  });
  // axis
  const np = pt(90 - spDecl), sp = pt(-90 - spDecl);
  const ext = 1.12;
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx + (np[0]-cx)*ext).attr("y1", cy + (np[1]-cy)*ext).attr("x2", cx + (sp[0]-cx)*ext).attr("y2", cy + (sp[1]-cy)*ext)
    .attr("stroke", "#e2e8f0").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + (np[0]-cx)*1.2).attr("y", cy + (np[1]-cy)*1.2).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 11).text("N");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + (sp[0]-cx)*1.2).attr("y", cy + (sp[1]-cy)*1.2 + 4).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 11).text("S");
  // background rays
  for (let y = cy - R; y <= cy + R; y += R / 5) {
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", 8).attr("y1", y).attr("x2", cx - Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, R*R - (y-cy)*(y-cy)))).attr("y2", y)
      .attr("stroke", "rgba(253,224,71,0.18)").attr("stroke-width", 1);
  }
  // beam
  const phi = spLocLat[spLoc];
  const ang = phi - spDecl;
  const E = spEnergy(phi, spDecl);
  const p = pt(ang);
  const h = R * 0.16;
  if (E > 0) {
    const y1 = p[1] - h/2, y2 = p[1] + h/2;
    const hitX = y => cx - Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, R*R - (y-cy)*(y-cy)));
    const yy1 = Math.max(y1, cy - R), yy2 = Math.min(y2, cy + R);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M 8 ${y1} L ${hitX(yy1)} ${yy1} A ${R} ${R} 0 0 0 ${hitX(yy2)} ${yy2} L 8 ${y2} Z`)
      .attr("fill", "rgba(253,224,71,0.55)").attr("stroke", "#fde047");
    const a1 = Math.asin(Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, (cy - yy1) / R))) / rad, a2 = Math.asin(Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, (cy - yy2) / R))) / rad;
    const q1 = pt(a1), q2 = pt(a2);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", `M ${q1[0]} ${q1[1]} A ${R} ${R} 0 0 0 ${q2[0]} ${q2[1]}`).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#f97316").attr("stroke-width", 6).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  } else {
    svg.append("text").attr("x", 14).attr("y", 22).attr("fill", "#fca5a5").attr("font-size", 12).text("This spot is in darkness or the light only grazes it.");
  }
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", p[0]).attr("cy", p[1]).attr("r", 4).attr("fill", "#fff");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 14).attr("y", H - 30).attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 12).text(`☀️ Sunlight from the left · ${spMonth}`);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 14).attr("y", H - 12).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 12).text(`Beam aimed at: ${spLoc}`);
  const spread = E > 0 ? (1361 / E) : Infinity;
  return html`<div style="max-width:560px;margin:auto;">${svg.node()}
  <div class="sp-readout"><b>Energy from the Sun:</b> 1,361 W/m² (the beam is the same everywhere)<br>
  <b>Energy received on Earth at ${spLoc}:</b> <span style="font-size:1.15em;font-weight:800;color:#f97316;">${E.toLocaleString()} W/m²</span>
  ${E > 0 ? html`<br>The orange arc shows the ground the beam covers: <b>${spread < 1.005 ? "the smallest possible area (direct rays)" : spread.toFixed(1) + "× as much ground"}</b> as a direct hit.` : html`<br>The beam's energy is spread over so much ground that almost nothing reaches each square meter.`}</div></div>`;
}
```

<p class="sp-caption">Model: noon sunlight at the top of the atmosphere, 1,361 W/m² × cos(angle from direct). Clouds and air are ignored.</p>

Energy received: North Pole **≈ 0**, Tropic of Cancer **≈ 1,249**, Equator **1,361**, Tropic of Capricorn **≈ 1,249**, South Pole **≈ 0**. (Your class simulator may show slightly different numbers. The pattern is what matters.)
- **Q2:** Energy from the Sun is the **same** at every location, but energy received on Earth is **highest at the equator** and **decreases toward both poles**.
- **Q3:** Near the equator the light hits **straight on** and is **concentrated** in a small area. Toward the poles it hits at a **low angle** and is **spread out** over a larger area.
- **Q4:** Yes. The **more spread out** the sunlight, the **less energy** each square meter receives.
:::

## See-Think-Wonder {#sp-stw1}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder

Fill in each row with what you **saw**, what you **think** explains it, and what you **wonder**:

1. Patterns in the **global average temperature** data
2. Patterns in the **amount of energy received** at different parts of the globe
3. Patterns in the **spread of sunlight** at different parts of the globe
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

| See | Think |
|---|---|
| Temperatures are **highest at the equator** and **decrease** toward either pole. | Places that get more energy from the Sun are warmer. |
| Energy received is **highest at the equator** and **decreases** toward either pole. | The angle the sunlight hits changes how much energy reaches each square meter. |
| Sunlight is **concentrated** near the equator and **spread out** near the poles. | Spread-out sunlight = less energy per area = colder temperatures. |

**Good "wonder" questions:** Why do we see **both** cold and warm air masses at fronts if they meet at one latitude? What makes some air masses **warm and moist** and others **cold and dry**? **Where** do the different air masses come from?
:::

::: {.key-idea}
**🔑 Key idea:** Earth is heated **unevenly**. Sunlight is most direct and concentrated near the **equator** and most spread out near the **poles**, so the tropics are warm and the poles are cold. That temperature difference is the starting point for air masses, wind and storms.
:::

- **Q2:** Earth is a **sphere**, so sunlight hits the equator **directly** (concentrated) and the poles at a **low angle** (spread out). The same amount of sunlight spread over a larger area delivers **less energy per square meter**.

## Part 2: What causes the characteristics of different air masses? {#sp-explain1-part2}

**Defining Air Masses:** Air masses are **very large parcels of air** that have the **same temperature and moisture** throughout. They develop in regions where the atmosphere is relatively **stable**, and they **take on the moisture and temperature characteristics of that region**.

| Air mass | Forms over… | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| **Continental Tropical (cT)** | land, low latitudes | dry and warm |
| **Maritime Polar (mP)** | ocean, high latitudes | moist and cold |
| **Continental Polar (cP)** | land, high latitudes | dry and cold |
| **Maritime Tropical (mT)** | ocean, low latitudes | moist and warm |

- **Continental** (c) = over **land** → **dry** (little water to evaporate)
- **Maritime** (m) = over **water** → **moist** (lots of evaporation)
- **Tropical** (T) = **low latitude**, direct sunlight → **warm**
- **Polar** (P) = **high latitude**, spread-out sunlight → **cold**

### ✏️ In your packet: Part 2 (Claims About the Origin of Air Masses)

- **Q1:** Summarize the key ideas about air masses **in your own words**.
- **Claims table:** For each air mass (Continental Tropical, Maritime Polar, Continental Polar, Maritime Tropical), write which **region(s) A–F** produce it (**claim**), your **evidence** (temperature map, sunlight model, the map), and the **reasoning** (science concept) that connects them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

| Air mass | Claim | Evidence | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Continental Tropical** (dry, warm) | **E** | E is desert land at about 30° N, where the map shows warm temperatures. | Direct sunlight → lots of energy → warm. Land → little water to evaporate → dry. |
| **Maritime Polar** (moist, cold) | **A and C** | A and C are oceans at about 50–60° N, where the map shows cool colors. | Spread-out sunlight → less energy → cold. Ocean → evaporation → moist. |
| **Continental Polar** (dry, cold) | **B** | B is land at about 60° N, where the map is blue/green (cold). | Little energy → cold. Frozen land → little evaporation → dry. |
| **Maritime Tropical** (moist, warm) | **D and F** | D and F are oceans near 20–30° N, where the map is orange/red. | Direct sunlight → warm. Warm water evaporates quickly → moist. |

**Big idea:** Air masses take on the characteristics of the region where they form. Cold, dry air from the north and warm, moist air from the south must somehow be **moving toward the US and colliding** there. *What moves them?* That's Explore 2.
:::

::: {.sp-note}
📝 **Note on the teacher guide:** one of its "Look and Listen For" bullets says warm **moist** air masses form over land in the southern latitudes. Air masses that form over warm **land** are warm and **dry** (continental tropical).
:::

::: {.key-idea}
**🔑 Key idea:** An air mass gets its **temperature from latitude** (how much sunlight it gets) and its **moisture from the surface** (land = dry, ocean = moist). The US sits between **cold, dry cP** air from Canada and **warm, moist mT** air from the Gulf of Mexico, which is perfect for winter storms.
:::

# Explore 2: Global Movement of Air Investigation {#sp-explore2}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🌬️ What Moves the Air Masses?

You found that cold air forms near the poles and warm air near the equator. But **what moves them** so they meet over the US, and **what steers** the storms? Investigate how air moves around the whole planet.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spGlobe = function({stage = 3, cells = true, winds = true, pressure = true, wet = false, labels = true} = {}) {
  const W = Math.min(width, 560), H = Math.round(W * 0.86);
  const R = Math.min(H * 0.43, (W - 34 - 62) / 2), cx = 34 + R, cy = H / 2;
  // schematic: latitude spaced evenly so the polar belts are visible
  const yAt = lat => cy - R * lat / 90;
  const half = lat => R * Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, 1 - (lat / 90) ** 2));
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Model of global circulation: pressure belts, surface winds and convection cells");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  [["spArW", "#ffffff"], ["spArC", "#fbbf24"], ["spArB", "#1e3a8a"]].forEach(([id, col]) => {
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 6).attr("refY", 5)
      .attr("markerWidth", 5).attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z").attr("fill", col);
  });
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1324");
  const clip = defs.append("clipPath").attr("id", "spGlobeClip");
  clip.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R);
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#1d4ed8");
  const g = svg.append("g").attr("clip-path", "url(#spGlobeClip)");
  if (wet) {
    const band = (a, b, col) => g.append("rect").attr("x", cx - R).attr("width", 2 * R).attr("y", yAt(b)).attr("height", yAt(a) - yAt(b)).attr("fill", col);
    [[-8, 8], [52, 68], [-68, -52]].forEach(([a, b]) => band(a, b, "rgba(56,189,248,0.55)"));
    [[22, 38], [-38, -22], [78, 90], [-90, -78]].forEach(([a, b]) => band(a, b, "rgba(250,204,21,0.45)"));
  }
  const latLines = stage === 1 ? [0] : stage === 2 ? [0, 30, -30] : [0, 30, -30, 60, -60];
  latLines.forEach(l => svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx - half(l)).attr("x2", cx + half(l)).attr("y1", yAt(l)).attr("y2", yAt(l))
    .attr("stroke", "rgba(255,255,255,0.75)").attr("stroke-dasharray", l === 0 ? null : "5,4"));
  [90, 60, 30, 0, -30, -60, -90].forEach(l => svg.append("text").attr("x", cx - R - 6).attr("y", yAt(l) + 4).attr("text-anchor", "end")
    .attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").attr("font-size", 10).text(l === 0 ? "0°" : `${Math.abs(l)}°${l > 0 ? "N" : "S"}`));
  if (wet) {
    [[0, "WET"], [60, "WET"], [-60, "WET"], [30, "DRY"], [-30, "DRY"], [84, "DRY"], [-84, "DRY"]].forEach(([l, t]) =>
      svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + half(l) * 0.55).attr("y", yAt(l) + 4).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10).attr("font-weight", 800)
        .attr("fill", t === "WET" ? "#e0f2fe" : "#fef9c3").text(t));
  }
  if (pressure) {
    const P = stage === 1 ? [[0, "L"], [90, "H"], [-90, "H"]] : stage === 2 ? [[0, "L"], [30, "H"], [-30, "H"]] : [[0, "L"], [30, "H"], [-30, "H"], [60, "L"], [-60, "L"], [90, "H"], [-90, "H"]];
    P.forEach(([l, t]) => svg.append("text").attr("x", Math.abs(l) > 80 ? cx : cx - half(l) * 0.55).attr("y", Math.abs(l) > 80 ? (l > 0 ? yAt(90) - 3 : yAt(-90) + 17) : yAt(l) + 6).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("font-size", 17).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", t === "H" ? "#fca5a5" : "#93c5fd").attr("stroke", "#0b1324").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text(t));
  }
  if (winds) {
    const belts = stage === 1
      ? [{a: 0, b: 90, d: [0, 1], name: "Surface air flows to the equator"}, {a: -90, b: 0, d: [0, -1], name: ""}]
      : [{a: 0, b: 30, d: [-1, 1], name: "NE trade winds"}, {a: 30, b: 60, d: [1, -1], name: "Westerlies"}, {a: -30, b: 0, d: [-1, -1], name: "SE trade winds"}, {a: -60, b: -30, d: [1, 1], name: "Westerlies"},
         ...(stage === 3 ? [{a: 60, b: 90, d: [-1, 1], name: "Polar easterlies"}, {a: -90, b: -60, d: [-1, -1], name: "Polar easterlies"}] : [])];
    belts.forEach(bt => {
      const rows = stage === 1 ? [15, 45, 70].map(f => bt.a + (bt.b - bt.a) * f / 90) : [Math.abs(bt.a + bt.b) > 140 ? Math.sign(bt.a + bt.b) * 76 : (bt.a + bt.b) / 2];
      rows.forEach(m => {
        const hw = half(m) * 0.8, len = Math.min(26, (yAt(bt.a) - yAt(bt.b)) * 0.38);
        const n = Math.hypot(bt.d[0], bt.d[1]);
        const xs = stage === 1 ? [-0.5, 0, 0.5] : Math.abs(m) > 65 ? [-0.55, 0.45] : [-0.45, 0.05, 0.55];
        xs.forEach(f => {
          const x0 = cx + f * hw, y0 = yAt(m);
          svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 - bt.d[0] / n * len / 2).attr("y1", y0 - bt.d[1] / n * len / 2)
            .attr("x2", x0 + bt.d[0] / n * len / 2).attr("y2", y0 + bt.d[1] / n * len / 2)
            .attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2.4).attr("marker-end", "url(#spArW)");
        });
      });
      const labLat = Math.abs(bt.a + bt.b) > 140 ? Math.sign(bt.a + bt.b) * 72 : (bt.a + bt.b) / 2;
      if (labels && bt.name) svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", stage === 1 ? yAt(60) - 10 : yAt(labLat) + (labLat > 0 ? -11 : 19))
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10.5).attr("font-weight", 700).attr("fill", "#fde68a")
        .attr("stroke", "#0b1324").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text(bt.name);
    });
  }
  if (cells) {
    const x0 = cx + R + 10, cw = Math.max(36, W - x0 - 14);
    const loops = stage === 1 ? [{a: 0, b: 88, name: "one big cell", inner: "eq"}, {a: -88, b: 0, name: "one big cell", inner: "eq"}]
      : [{a: 0, b: 30, name: "Hadley", inner: "eq"}, {a: -30, b: 0, name: "Hadley", inner: "eq"}, {a: 30, b: 60, name: "Ferrel", inner: "pole"}, {a: -60, b: -30, name: "Ferrel", inner: "pole"},
         ...(stage === 3 ? [{a: 60, b: 88, name: "Polar", inner: "eq"}, {a: -88, b: -60, name: "Polar", inner: "eq"}] : [])];
    loops.forEach(L => {
      const yTop = yAt(Math.max(L.a, L.b)) + 3, yBot = yAt(Math.min(L.a, L.b)) - 3;
      svg.append("rect").attr("x", x0).attr("y", yTop).attr("width", cw).attr("height", yBot - yTop).attr("rx", Math.min(14, (yBot - yTop) / 2))
        .attr("fill", "rgba(251,191,36,0.12)").attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
      // equatorward edge of this loop is closer to 0°
      const north = L.a >= 0;
      const eqY = north ? yBot : yTop, poleY = north ? yTop : yBot;
      // surface (inner/left side): toward equator if inner == "eq"
      const toEq = L.inner === "eq";
      const ySurfFrom = toEq ? poleY : eqY, ySurfTo = toEq ? eqY : poleY;
      const shrink = (a, b) => [a + (b - a) * 0.22, a + (b - a) * 0.78];
      const [s1, s2] = shrink(ySurfFrom, ySurfTo), [u1, u2] = shrink(ySurfTo, ySurfFrom);
      svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 + 7).attr("x2", x0 + 7).attr("y1", s1).attr("y2", s2).attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("marker-end", "url(#spArC)");
      svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 + cw - 7).attr("x2", x0 + cw - 7).attr("y1", u1).attr("y2", u2).attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("marker-end", "url(#spArC)");
      if (cw > 50 && Math.abs(yBot - yTop) > 34) svg.append("text").attr("x", x0 + cw / 2).attr("y", (yTop + yBot) / 2 + 4).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10).attr("fill", "#fde68a").text(L.name);
    });
    svg.append("text").attr("x", W - 6).attr("y", 12).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("font-size", 9.5).attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").text("cells: left = surface, right = aloft");
  }
  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
  const out = html`<div class="sp-readout"></div>`;
  btn.onclick = () => {

    out.innerHTML = `<b>${n} of ${tot} correct.</b> ${n === tot ? "🎉 Notice the pattern: collide → rising → low → wet, and move apart → sinking → high → dry." : "Red cells need another look. Hint: find the H's and L's on the cross-section first."}`;
  };
  fill.onclick = () => { cellsRef.forEach(([row, r]) => ["w", "v", "p", "r"].forEach(k => { r[k].value = row[k]; r[k].style.background = "#e0e7ff"; })); out.innerHTML = "Answers filled in. Look for the pattern in each row."; };
  const wrap = html`<div style="max-width:640px;margin:auto;"><div class="sp-scroll"></div></div>`;
  wrap.querySelector(".sp-scroll").appendChild(table);
  wrap.appendChild(btn); wrap.appendChild(fill); wrap.appendChild(out);
  return wrap;
}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Table 3 and the second See-Think-Wonder

- **Table 3:** For each latitude, record whether surface winds **collide or move apart**, whether air is **rising or sinking**, whether pressure is **high or low**, and whether it is **wet or dry**.
- **See-Think-Wonder:** What patterns do you see in the **relationships between variables** in the table? What do you think explains them?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Table 3:** North Pole, 30° N, 30° S and South Pole: winds **move apart**, air **sinks**, **high** pressure, **dry**. 60° N, equator and 60° S: winds **collide**, air **rises**, **low** pressure, **wet**.
- **Patterns:** collide ↔ rising ↔ low pressure ↔ wet; move apart ↔ sinking ↔ high pressure ↔ dry. The pattern **repeats** every 30° and is the **same in both hemispheres**.
- **Explanations to look for:** Air **rises at the equator** because it gets the most energy from the Sun, warms and becomes **less dense**. Air **sinks at 30°** because, high up, it has cooled and become **denser**. Surface air **moves from high pressure toward low pressure**. The wind **curves** (right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern), maybe because **Earth is spinning**.
- **Good "wonder" questions:** Do these winds move air masses? Is this why warm and cold air masses meet over the US? Is this why blizzard and hurricane paths curve?
:::

::: {.sp-note}
📝 **Note on the teacher guide:** its sample explanation says air sinks at 30° because "its density decreases." Cooling makes air **denser** (its density **increases**), and denser air sinks. Another bullet says winds curve "to the left in the northern hemisphere." It's the reverse: **right** in the Northern Hemisphere and **left** in the Southern (the same guide states this correctly in Explain 2).
:::

## Part 2: Why does air curve as it travels north and south? {#sp-explore2-part2}

**Using a model to explain why global winds bend.** In class, partners draw on a spinning balloon. Here's a virtual balloon. You are looking straight down on one pole. The pen moves in a **straight line** from the pole toward the equator while the balloon spins under it. Watch the line it leaves on the balloon.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spBalView = Inputs.radio(["North Pole view", "South Pole view"], {label: "Look from:", value: "North Pole view"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spBalDir = Inputs.radio(["Normal (left to right, like Earth)", "Reversed"], {label: "Spin the balloon:", value: "Normal (left to right, like Earth)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spBalGo = Inputs.button("✏️ Draw the line")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  spBalGo;
  const W = Math.min(width, 420), H = W, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = W * 0.42;
  const north = spBalView.startsWith("North"), normal = spBalDir.startsWith("Normal");
  // visual spin: from above the North Pole Earth spins counterclockwise; from the South Pole it looks clockwise
  const ccw = north === normal;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Balloon seen from above one pole, with a pen line drawn from the pole to the equator while it spins");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1324");
  const disk = svg.append("g");
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#f472b6").attr("stroke", "#9d174d").attr("stroke-width", 2);
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R * 0.97).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#1e293b").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  for (let k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    const a = k * Math.PI / 4;
    disk.append("line").attr("x1", cx).attr("y1", cy).attr("x2", cx + R * Math.cos(a)).attr("y2", cy + R * Math.sin(a)).attr("stroke", "rgba(255,255,255,0.35)");
  }
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx + R * 0.6).attr("cy", cy - R * 0.3).attr("r", 9).attr("fill", "#fde047");
  const trace = disk.append("path").attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#1d4ed8").attr("stroke-width", 4).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx).attr("y1", cy).attr("x2", cx).attr("y2", cy + R).attr("stroke", "#e2e8f0").attr("stroke-dasharray", "5,4").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  const pen = svg.append("circle").attr("r", 7).attr("fill", "#22c55e").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", cy - 6).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fff").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", 700).text(north ? "N. Pole" : "S. Pole");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 18).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 12).text(`Spinning ${ccw ? "counterclockwise ↺" : "clockwise ↻"}`);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", H - 10).attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").attr("font-size", 11).text("Dashed line = the pen's straight path · edge = equator");
  const T = 3500, maxDeg = 100;
  const pts = [];
  const t0 = performance.now();
  let raf;
  const step = (now) => {
    const t = Math.min(1, (now - t0) / T);
    const rot = (ccw ? -1 : 1) * maxDeg * t;            // SVG degrees (positive = clockwise on screen)
    const r = R * 0.95 * t;
    const a = -rot * Math.PI / 180;                     // undo the spin to get the balloon-frame position
    const x = 0, y = r;
    pts.push([cx + x * Math.cos(a) - y * Math.sin(a), cy + x * Math.sin(a) + y * Math.cos(a)]);
    disk.attr("transform", `rotate(${rot},${cx},${cy})`);
    trace.attr("d", d3.line()(pts));
    pen.attr("cy", cy + r);
    if (t < 1) raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  };
  raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  const bend = ccw ? "right" : "left";
  const note = html`<div class="sp-readout" style="max-width:420px;margin:6px auto;">From the ${north ? "North" : "South"} Pole, the balloon spins <b>${ccw ? "counterclockwise" : "clockwise"}</b>. The pen moves straight, but the line on the balloon <b>bends to the ${bend}</b> of the direction the pen is moving.</div>`;
  return html`<div style="max-width:420px;margin:auto;">${svg.node()}${note}</div>`;
}
```

<p class="sp-caption">Tap "Draw the line" again after changing the view or the spin direction.</p>

```{ojs}
  {q: "You drew a straight line from the North Pole toward the equator while the balloon spun normally. Which way did the line bend?",
   options: ["To the right of the direction the pen moved", "To the left", "It stayed perfectly straight", "It bent toward the North Pole"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "The balloon's surface slides under the pen, so the mark ends up curving to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. That's the Coriolis effect."},
  {q: "What do you predict if the balloon spins the opposite direction?",
   options: ["The line bends the same way", "The bends flip: left in the Northern Hemisphere and right in the Southern", "No line appears", "The line bends toward the pole"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The bending comes from the spin. Reverse the spin and the bending reverses. Try it with the Reversed setting."}
])
```

## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

**Analysis:** (1) **Counterclockwise**. (2) **Clockwise**. (3–4) The line **curved**: it bent to the **right** of the direction it was drawn. (5–6) It curved to the **left**. (7) The bends would **flip**: left in the north, right in the south. (8) The surface **moves underneath** air (or the pen) as it travels north or south, so its path **appears to bend**: right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern. That's what the global winds did in the animation.

**Reliability:** (1) A balloon is smaller, smoother, often not a perfect sphere, has no atmosphere, oceans or mountains, and is spun by hand at an uneven speed. (2) **Yes, for this purpose**: it shows the key cause (a spinning, curved surface moving under a moving object) and gives the right bending directions. It can't show wind speeds or exact paths. (3) You assume the **spin of the balloon behaves like Earth's rotation** (same direction, steady) and that **air moving toward a storm's center bends the same way** as the pen line. Models always make assumptions and approximations. Keep that in mind when you judge **climate models** later!
:::

::: {.key-idea}
**🔑 Key idea:** Global winds come from **uneven heating** (air rises where it's warm and sinks where it's cold, making pressure belts), **pressure differences** (surface air flows from high to low pressure), and **Earth's rotation** (the **Coriolis effect** bends winds right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern).
:::

# Explain 2: Explaining Global Wind Patterns {#sp-explain2}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧠 Building a Causal Model of Global Winds

Now explain **why** the patterns from Explore 2 happen. Your model should include what happens to **air and water at the molecular level** when they are heated and cooled.
:::


<p class="sp-caption">Winds are named for the direction they come <b>from</b>: the "NE trades" blow from the northeast toward the southwest; the westerlies (the packet's "S.W. winds") blow from the southwest toward the northeast.</p>

## Part 1: Explaining High and Low Pressure Bands at Earth's Surface {#sp-explain2-part1}

The packet's diagram shows **low** pressure at **0°, 60° N and 60° S**, and **high** pressure at **30° N, 30° S, 90° N and 90° S**.

**What's happening to the molecules?**

- **Heating** makes air molecules move **faster** and spread **farther apart** → the air **expands**, becomes **less dense** and **rises**. Rising air leaves **fewer molecules pressing down** on the surface → **low pressure**.
- **Cooling** makes molecules move **slower** and pack **closer together** → the air **contracts**, becomes **denser** and **sinks**. Sinking air piles **more molecules** onto the surface → **high pressure**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spQuiz("sp-pressure-quiz", "Check: Pressure Bands", [
  {q: "Why is surface pressure LOW at the equator?",
   options: ["Air is sinking there", "Direct sunlight heats the air; it expands, becomes less dense and rises, so less air presses on the surface", "There is no air at the equator", "The equator is at a high altitude"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Table 3 shows rising air at the equator. Rising, less dense air means lower pressure at the surface."},
  {q: "Why is surface pressure HIGH near 30° N?",
   options: ["Air that rose at the equator cools high up, becomes denser and sinks near 30°, piling up at the surface", "Warm ocean water pushes the air up", "The Sun is directly overhead at 30° N all year", "Mountains are tallest at 30° N"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Air rising at the equator spreads poleward at the top of the troposphere, cools, gets denser and sinks around 30°: high pressure."}
])
```

For each: **claim**, **evidence** (a pattern from Table 3) and **reasoning** (science concepts).
:::

| | Claim | Evidence | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low (0°, 60°)** | Pressure is low because air is **rising** there. | Table 3: surface winds **collide** and air **rises** at 0°, 60° N, 60° S. | At the equator, strong sunlight heats air; molecules speed up and spread out, so the air is **less dense** and rises. At 60°, surface winds meet and the **warmer westerlies are forced up** over colder polar air. Rising air means less weight of air on the surface. |
| **High (30°, 90°)** | Pressure is high because air is **sinking** there. | Table 3: surface winds **move apart** and air **sinks** at 30° and the poles. | Air high in the troposphere **cools**; molecules slow down and pack closer, so the air is **denser** and sinks. At the poles, very cold air is dense and sinks. Sinking air adds weight to the surface. |
:::

## Part 2: Explaining the General Direction of Wind at Earth's Surface {#sp-explain2-part2}

Two questions, two causes:

- **North/south part of the wind:** surface air flows **from high pressure to low pressure** (from 30° toward 0° and toward 60°; from the poles toward 60°).
- **East/west part of the wind:** Earth's rotation bends moving air. This is the **Coriolis effect**: moving objects and winds **appear to bend** as they move across a rotating surface, because different latitudes move at **different speeds** as Earth spins (fastest at the equator, zero at the poles). Winds bend **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and **left in the Southern Hemisphere**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spCorLat = Inputs.range([0, 90], {label: "Latitude (°N)", step: 5, value: 40})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const v = 1670 * Math.cos(spCorLat * Math.PI / 180);
  const rows = [0, 30, 40.7, 60, 90].map(l => ({lat: l, v: 1670 * Math.cos(l * Math.PI / 180), name: l === 40.7 ? "NYC" : `${l}°`}));
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    title: "How fast does the ground move east as Earth spins?",
    width: Math.min(width, 520), height: 230, marginLeft: 46, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {domain: [0, 90], label: "Latitude (° N)"}, y: {domain: [0, 1800], label: "Eastward speed (km/h)", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(d3.range(0, 91, 1).map(l => ({l, v: 1670 * Math.cos(l * Math.PI / 180)})), {x: "l", y: "v", stroke: "#3949ab", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "lat", y: "v", r: 3.5, fill: "#3949ab"}),
      Plot.text(rows, {x: "lat", y: "v", text: "name", dy: -10, fontSize: 10, fill: "currentColor"}),
      Plot.dot([{l: spCorLat, v}], {x: "l", y: "v", r: 7, fill: "#f97316", stroke: "white"})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div style="max-width:520px;margin:auto;">${chart}<div class="sp-readout">At <b>${spCorLat}° N</b> the ground moves east at about <b>${Math.round(v).toLocaleString()} km/h</b>. Air moving <b>toward the equator</b> travels over faster-moving ground, so it falls behind and bends <b>west</b> (the trade winds blow from the NE). Air moving <b>toward the poles</b> keeps its extra eastward speed and bends <b>east</b> (the westerlies).</div></div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
   correct: 1,
```

You can annotate the diagram to make your thinking visible.

## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **North/south. Claim:** Surface winds move from **high-pressure** latitudes to **low-pressure** latitudes. **Evidence:** Table 3 shows high pressure at 30° and 90° and low pressure at 0° and 60°; the winds blow from 30° toward 0° and 60°, and from the poles toward 60°. **Reasoning:** Air at high pressure is denser (more molecules packed together), so it **pushes outward** toward areas with fewer molecules (low pressure).
- **East/west. Claim:** The winds bend because **Earth rotates** (the Coriolis effect). **Evidence:** In the animation, winds curved; in the balloon model, a straight line bent **right** in the north and **left** in the south. **Reasoning:** Earth's surface moves east at different speeds at different latitudes. Air moving across that rotating surface **appears to bend**, so equator-bound air becomes the **trade winds** (from the east) and pole-bound air becomes the **westerlies** (from the west).
:::

## Part 3: Explaining Winds in Local Storm Systems {#sp-explain2-part3}

The Coriolis effect doesn't just bend global winds. It also shapes the winds in **local low-pressure storm systems**. Follow the packet steps with the model below.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spLowStep = Inputs.radio(["Step 1: arrows toward the L", "Step 2: bend each arrow", "Step 3: the overall shape"], {label: "Show:", value: "Step 1: arrows toward the L"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spLowHemi = Inputs.radio(["Northern Hemisphere", "Southern Hemisphere"], {label: "Hemisphere:", value: "Northern Hemisphere"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 380), H = W, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R1 = W * 0.42, R2 = W * 0.22;
  const nh = spLowHemi.startsWith("Northern"), step = +spLowStep[5];
  const turn = (nh ? 1 : -1) * 65 * Math.PI / 180;    // + = right turn on screen (y down)
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Winds flowing toward a low pressure center and bending to form a spiral");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  [["spLa", "#1d4ed8"], ["spLb", "#dc2626"], ["spLc", "#7c3aed"]].forEach(([id, c]) => defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 6).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5).attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto").append("path").attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z").attr("fill", c));
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#f1f5f9");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", cy + 14).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 42).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", "#b91c1c").text("L");
  if (step < 3) {
    for (let k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
      const th = k * Math.PI / 4;
      const x1 = cx + R1 * Math.cos(th), y1 = cy + R1 * Math.sin(th), x2 = cx + R2 * Math.cos(th), y2 = cy + R2 * Math.sin(th);
      svg.append("line").attr("x1", x1).attr("y1", y1).attr("x2", x2).attr("y2", y2).attr("stroke", "#1d4ed8").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#spLa)");
      if (step === 2) {
        const dx = -Math.cos(th), dy = -Math.sin(th);
        const ex = dx * Math.cos(turn) - dy * Math.sin(turn), ey = dx * Math.sin(turn) + dy * Math.cos(turn);
        const L = W * 0.11;
        svg.append("line").attr("x1", x2).attr("y1", y2).attr("x2", x2 + ex * L).attr("y2", y2 + ey * L).attr("stroke", "#dc2626").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#spLb)");
      }
    }
  } else {
    for (let k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
      const pts = d3.range(0, 1.001, 0.02).map(f => {
        const r = R1 * (1 - 0.78 * f), th = k * Math.PI / 2 + (nh ? -1 : 1) * f * 2.4;
        return [cx + r * Math.cos(th), cy + r * Math.sin(th)];
      });
      svg.append("path").attr("d", d3.line().curve(d3.curveBasis)(pts)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7c3aed").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#spLc)");
    }
  }
  const msg = step === 1 ? "Wind moves <b>toward</b> low pressure (from high to low)."
    : step === 2 ? `Each arrow bends to the <b>${nh ? "right" : "left"}</b> (${nh ? "Northern" : "Southern"} Hemisphere).`
    : `The bent arrows make a <b>${nh ? "counterclockwise" : "clockwise"}</b> spiral into the low.`;
  const d = html`<div style="max-width:380px;margin:auto;"></div>`;
  d.appendChild(svg.node());
  const p = html`<div class="sp-readout"></div>`; p.innerHTML = msg; d.appendChild(p);
  return d;
}
```

```{ojs}
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Inflowing air from every side turns right and misses the center, sweeping around it counterclockwise."},
  {q: "Predict: how would a tropical cyclone near Australia (Southern Hemisphere) spin?",
   options: ["Counterclockwise, the same as in the north", "Clockwise, because winds bend to the left in the Southern Hemisphere", "It wouldn't spin", "It would spin in random directions"],
```

7. Air flows in toward the low from all sides, but the Coriolis effect bends each stream to the **right**, so instead of crashing straight into the center it swirls around it **counterclockwise**.
**Predict:** In the Southern Hemisphere air bends **left**, so cyclones spin **clockwise**. (Winter storms over the US are lows too, so they also spin counterclockwise.)

## Part 4: Explaining Patterns of Precipitation on a Global Level {#sp-explain2-part4}

Turn on **Wet and dry bands** in the model above. Wet bands sit on the **low-pressure** belts (0°, 60°); dry bands on the **high-pressure** belts (30°, poles). Many of the world's great deserts (the Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the deserts of Australia and the southwest US) are near **30° N and 30° S**.

**Water molecules in rising and sinking air:**

- **Rising air** expands and **cools**. Water vapor molecules slow down and stick together: they **condense** into cloud droplets (releasing heat). Droplets grow → **rain or snow**.
- **Sinking air** is compressed and **warms**. Droplets **evaporate**, so clouds can't form → **dry**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spQuiz("sp-precip-quiz", "Check: Wet and Dry Bands", [
  {q: "Why is it so rainy near the equator?",
   options: ["Warm, moist air rises there, cools, and its water vapor condenses into clouds and rain", "Sinking air squeezes out the rain", "The equator is closest to the Sun", "Wind blows rain from the poles"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Rising air (Table 3: low pressure, rising) cools as it goes up. Cooler air can't hold as much water vapor, so it condenses."},
  {q: "Many deserts lie near 30° N. Which explanation fits the global wind model?",
   options: ["Air sinks there, warms as it is compressed, and clouds evaporate", "It's too cold for rain at 30°", "Winds collide there and push rain away", "There are no oceans at 30°"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "The 30° belts are high pressure with sinking air, so they are dry."}
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Part 4 and the model questions

1. Why do the **Wet** latitudes get a great deal of precipitation? (Claim, evidence from Table 3, reasoning.)
2. Why do the **Dry** latitudes get very little precipitation?

Then:

1. What **limitations** are there in the models we have looked at so far? How are they different from the real globe? What are they ignoring?
2. How might winds behave **differently on Earth** than in the model? Explain.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Wet. Claim:** Wet latitudes get lots of precipitation because air **rises** there. **Evidence:** Table 3: winds **collide**, air **rises**, pressure is **low** at 0° and 60°. **Reasoning:** Rising air cools; water vapor molecules lose energy and **condense** into droplets that fall as rain or snow.
- **Dry. Claim:** Dry latitudes get little precipitation because air **sinks** there. **Evidence:** Table 3: winds **move apart**, air **sinks**, pressure is **high** at 30° and 90°. **Reasoning:** Sinking air warms, so water stays as vapor (droplets evaporate) and clouds don't form.
- **Limitations:** The models show smooth, straight belts. They ignore **continents and oceans** (land heats faster than water), **mountains**, **seasons** (the belts shift north in July and south in January), and day-to-day **weather systems**. Real winds **wiggle and change**: the jet stream meanders, highs and lows move, and local winds (like sea breezes) form. The models are averages.
:::

## Summary Task {#sp-summary-task}

::: {.key-idea}
**🔑 The class consensus model (key points):**

1. The region at and near the **equator** gets the most **direct sunlight**. Air particles warm and spread out, so the air **expands**, becomes **less dense**, and a pressure difference makes surface air **converge** there and be forced **upward**.
2. As moist, warm air **rises it cools**, and its water vapor **condenses** to form **clouds**. This is where **rain** often falls.
3. The air reaches the top of the troposphere (a natural semi-barrier), **spreads outward**, keeps **cooling** and becomes **denser**, so it **sinks at 30° N and 30° S**.
4. Air reaching the **poles** high up keeps cooling, becomes denser and **sinks**.
5. As air moves across Earth's surface, Earth's **spin** bends it **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and **left in the Southern Hemisphere** (the Coriolis effect).
:::

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Explain: Summary Task

1. In the models the class developed, what **science concepts** were most useful in explaining what causes global wind and precipitation patterns?
2. How will you use your answer to Q1 when developing models for **other phenomena**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. The most useful concepts: **energy from the Sun** heats Earth unevenly; **heating and cooling change the motion and spacing of molecules**, which changes **density** (warm air rises, cool air sinks); **pressure differences** push air from high to low; **condensation** of water vapor as air cools; and **Earth's rotation** (Coriolis effect).
2. Next time, start with the **small scale** (what molecules of air and water are doing as energy moves in or out) to explain what you see at the **large scale** (winds, clouds, storms). Track **where energy and matter flow** in the system. You'll need this for your hurricane model in the next chapter.
:::

```{ojs}
    ...[30, 60].map(l => Plot.geo({type: "LineString", coordinates: d3.range(-140, 1, 2).map(x => [x, l])}, {stroke: "#475569", strokeDasharray: "5,4"})),
    Plot.text([{x: -127, y: 28, t: "30° N high"}, {x: -127, y: 62.5, t: "60° N low"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 10, fill: "#334155", textAnchor: "start"}),
    showW ? Plot.link(arrows, {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2, markerEnd: "arrow"}) : null,
    showW ? Plot.text([{x: -52, y: 22.5, t: "NE trade winds"}, {x: -52, y: 36.5, t: "Westerlies"}, {x: -52, y: 57, t: "Polar easterlies"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: 700, fill: "#0f172a", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3}) : null,
    showA ? Plot.text(am, {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fontSize: 10.5, fontWeight: 700, fill: "#7c2d12", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3}) : null,
    Plot.line(lines, {x: "x", y: "y", z: "id", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 3, curve: "catmull-rom", markerEnd: "arrow"}),
    Plot.dot([{x: -74, y: 40.7}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5, fill: "#f97316", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.text([{x: -74, y: 40.7}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "NYC", dx: 16, dy: 8, fontWeight: 800, fontSize: 11, fill: "#9a3412", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3})
  ].filter(Boolean);
  return Plot.plot({
    title: "Wind belts steer storms (schematic paths)",
    subtitle: "Blue = typical winter storm paths · Red = typical Atlantic hurricane paths",
    width: Math.min(width, 680), height: Math.round(Math.min(width, 680) * (width < 500 ? 0.72 : 0.6)),
    projection: {type: "equirectangular", domain: {type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: width < 500 ? [[-128, 8], [-35, 66]] : [[-130, 8], [-15, 66]]}},
    style: {background: "#cfe8f7", color: "#1e293b"},
    marks
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spQuiz("sp-steer-quiz", "Check: Storm Paths", [
  {q: "Why do so many winter storms form over the US?",
   options: ["The US is in the tropics", "The US sits between cold, dry cP air from Canada and warm, moist mT air from the Gulf. Global winds bring them together along the polar front", "Mountains create storms", "The Atlantic Ocean pulls storms toward it"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Cold air flows south from Canada and warm, moist air flows north from the Gulf. Where they collide, the warm air is forced up, cools and makes snow: a winter storm."},
  {q: "A hurricane forms near 15° N off Africa. Why does it first move west, then curve north and northeast?",
   options: ["The trade winds push it west; once it reaches about 30° N, the westerlies carry it northeast", "The Gulf Stream drags it", "It is pulled by the Moon", "Hurricanes always move toward land"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "In the trade-wind belt (0–30° N), winds blow from the east. North of the 30° high, the westerlies blow from the west and turn storms toward the northeast."}
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Elaborate Part 1

1. Use what you know about **how winter storms form**, **where air masses come from**, and **global winds at different latitudes** to explain **why so many winter storms form over the US**.
2. Use global wind patterns and the **2016–2017 US Winter Storms** map to explain the **path of blizzards** over the US.
3. Use global wind patterns, the **2020 Atlantic Tropical Storms** chart and the **Model of Generalized Planetary Wind Belts** to explain the **path of hurricanes** in the North Atlantic and eastern US.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. **Cold, dry (cP)** air forms over land in northern Canada and the Arctic and is carried **south** toward the US (the polar easterlies blow from the northeast). **Warm, moist (mT)** air forms over the Gulf of Mexico and the ocean near 30° N and is carried **north** toward the US by the **westerlies** (which blow from the southwest). They **meet along the polar front** over the US. Warm air is forced up over the cold air, cools and its water vapor condenses into snow: a winter storm.
2. Over the US (about 30–50° N) the **westerlies** blow from the **southwest toward the northeast**, so winter storms are carried **west to east** across the country and curve **northeast**, many passing over the Northeast and NYC.
3. Hurricanes form over warm water around **10–20° N**. The **NE trade winds** push them **west** across the Atlantic toward the Caribbean. Near **30° N** they curve **north** around the subtropical high, then the **westerlies** carry them **northeast**, sometimes up the East Coast (in 2020, a record 30 named storms formed in the Atlantic).
:::

::: {.sp-note}
📝 **Note on the teacher guide:** its sample ideas say cold air is carried down by winds that "move south west" and warm air by winds that "move north east" (correct), but also that the air masses meet "near the northwest region of the US" and that winds "that move north west" drive the storms. The storms are driven toward the **northeast** by the westerlies, and US winter storms most often hit the **central and northeastern** US.
:::

## Part 2: Making Predictions about the Trajectory of Winter Storm Jonas {#sp-elaborate-part2}

**Why predict storm paths?** Forecasts tell people **how and when to prepare**: when to stock up, close schools, pre-salt roads, and move cars off snow routes. Winter Storm Jonas (January 22–24, 2016) dropped a record **27.5 in** of snow on Central Park, the most in NYC since records began in 1869.

In the [Blizzards](unit5-blizzards.qmd) Evaluate, you found Jonas on the **Jan 21, 2016, 15 UTC** surface map. Now **forecast** where it went. Tap the map to place your prediction, then check it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 620), H = Math.round(W * 0.66);
  const stages = [
    {from: {lon: -95.5, lat: 30.5, t: "Jan 21, 15 UTC"}, to: {lon: -74.8, lat: 35.3, t: "Jan 23, 3 UTC"}, ask: "Two-day forecast: where was the low 2 days later (Jan 23, 3 UTC)?", hint: "Surface winds at this latitude are the westerlies (from the southwest)."},
    {from: {lon: -74.8, lat: 35.3, t: "Jan 23, 3 UTC"}, to: {lon: -73.8, lat: 36.5, t: "Jan 23, 9 UTC"}, ask: "6-hour forecast: where will the low be at 9 UTC?", hint: "Winds along the cold front blow from the southwest. The storm was slowing down and strengthening."},
    {from: {lon: -73.8, lat: 36.5, t: "Jan 23, 9 UTC"}, to: {lon: -72.9, lat: 37.6, t: "Jan 23, 15 UTC"}, ask: "6-hour forecast: where will the low be at 15 UTC?", hint: "Keep following the southwest winds, but the storm is moving slowly."}
  ];
  const proj = d3.geoConicConformal().parallels([30, 45]).rotate([88, 0])
    .fitExtent([[8, 8], [W - 8, H - 8]], {type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: [[-104, 24], [-62, 24], [-106, 47], [-60, 47]]})
    .clipExtent([[0, 0], [W, H]]);
  const path = d3.geoPath(proj);
  const hav = (a, b) => { const r = Math.PI / 180, dLat = (b.lat - a.lat) * r, dLon = (b.lon - a.lon) * r; const s = Math.sin(dLat/2)**2 + Math.cos(a.lat*r)*Math.cos(b.lat*r)*Math.sin(dLon/2)**2; return 2 * 6371 * Math.asin(Math.sqrt(s)); };
  let k = 0, guess = null, revealed = false;
  const history = [stages[0].from];
  const wrap = html`<div style="max-width:620px;margin:auto;"></div>`;
  const ask = html`<div class="sp-readout" style="font-weight:700;"></div>`;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H).style("cursor", "crosshair").style("touch-action", "manipulation")
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Map of the eastern United States for placing a forecast of Winter Storm Jonas");
  const btns = html`<div style="display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-top:8px;"></div>`;
  const check = html`<button style="min-height:44px;padding:8px 18px;border:none;border-radius:22px;background:#3949ab;color:#fff;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;">Check my forecast</button>`;
  const next = html`<button style="min-height:44px;padding:8px 18px;border:1.5px solid #3949ab;border-radius:22px;background:#fff;color:#3949ab;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;display:none;">Next forecast →</button>`;
  const out = html`<div class="sp-readout"></div>`;
  btns.appendChild(check); btns.appendChild(next);
  function draw() {
    svg.selectAll("*").remove();
    svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#bfdbfe");
    if (spLand) svg.append("path").attr("d", path(spLand)).attr("fill", "#f1e7cf").attr("stroke", "#8d7b5a").attr("stroke-width", 0.6);
    if (spStates) svg.append("path").attr("d", path(spStates)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#a8a29e").attr("stroke-width", 0.5);
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(d3.geoGraticule().step([10, 10])())).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#64748b").attr("stroke-opacity", 0.25);
    const nyc = proj([-74, 40.7]);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", nyc[0]).attr("cy", nyc[1]).attr("r", 4).attr("fill", "#0f172a");
    svg.append("text").attr("x", nyc[0] + 6).attr("y", nyc[1] - 4).attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", 700).attr("fill", "#0f172a").text("NYC");
    if (history.length > 1) svg.append("path").attr("d", d3.line()(history.map(p => proj([p.lon, p.lat])))).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#b91c1c").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("stroke-dasharray", "6,4");
    history.forEach((p, i) => {
      const [x, y] = proj([p.lon, p.lat]);
      const showLabel = i === 0 || i === history.length - 1;
      svg.append("text").attr("x", x).attr("y", y + 7).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 20).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", "#b91c1c").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text("L");
      if (showLabel) svg.append("text").attr("x", x + 10).attr("y", y + 20).attr("font-size", 10).attr("fill", "#7f1d1d").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text(p.t);
    });
    if (guess) {
      const [x, y] = proj([guess.lon, guess.lat]);
      svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", y).attr("r", 8).attr("fill", "#22c55e").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2);
      svg.append("text").attr("x", x).attr("y", y - 12).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10).attr("font-weight", 700).attr("fill", "#14532d").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text("my forecast");
    }
    if (k < stages.length) ask.innerHTML = `${k + 1}/3 · ${stages[k].ask}<br><span style="font-weight:400;">💡 ${stages[k].hint}</span>`;
    else ask.innerHTML = "Done! The low crawled northeast off the Mid-Atlantic coast, close enough for NYC to get heavy snow, then moved out to sea past New England on Jan 24.";
  }
  svg.on("click", (event) => {
    if (k >= stages.length || revealed) return;
    const ll = proj.invert(d3.pointer(event));
    if (!ll) return;
    guess = {lon: ll[0], lat: ll[1]};
    draw();
  });
  check.onclick = () => {
    if (k >= stages.length || revealed) return;
    if (!guess) { out.innerHTML = "👆 Tap the map first to place your forecast."; return; }
    const st = stages[k], km = hav(guess, st.to);
    history.push(st.to); revealed = true;
    const dir = guess.lon < st.from.lon - 0.3 && st.to.lon > st.from.lon ? " Your forecast went west, but the storm moved east with the westerlies." : "";
    out.innerHTML = `Actual (approximate) position at <b>${st.to.t}</b>: <b>${st.to.lat.toFixed(1)}° N, ${Math.abs(st.to.lon).toFixed(1)}° W</b>. Your forecast was about <b>${Math.round(km)} km (${Math.round(km * 0.621)} miles)</b> away.${km < 250 ? " 🎯 Great forecast!" : ""}${dir}`;
    guess = null; draw();
    check.style.display = "none"; next.style.display = k < stages.length - 1 ? "inline-block" : "none";
    if (k === stages.length - 1) { k++; draw(); }
  };
  next.onclick = () => { k++; revealed = false; out.innerHTML = ""; check.style.display = "inline-block"; next.style.display = "none"; draw(); };
  draw();
  wrap.appendChild(ask); wrap.appendChild(svg.node()); wrap.appendChild(btns); wrap.appendChild(out);
  return wrap;
}
```

<p class="sp-caption">Low-pressure positions are approximate, estimated from the storm's reported track. Your teacher's surface maps for 3, 9 and 15 UTC on Jan 23 show the exact positions. UTC is 5 hours ahead of New York time in winter, so 15 UTC = 10 a.m. in NYC.</p>

```{ojs}
   options: ["Farther west, over Arizona", "Northeast, off the Mid-Atlantic coast, because the westerlies carry storms from southwest to northeast", "Straight north into Canada", "Stays in Texas"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "At about 30–40° N, the westerlies push weather systems east and northeast. Jonas crossed the Southeast and reached the ocean off North Carolina by Jan 23."},
  {q: "Between 3 UTC and 15 UTC on Jan 23, Jonas moved only about 300 km. Why does that matter for NYC?",
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Elaborate Part 2

**Two-day forecast:** (1) Use **surface wind patterns on a global scale** to predict where Jonas was **2 days later**. (2) Mark it on your map. (3) Check against the **3 UTC, Jan 23** map. How close were you?

**Next several hours:** (1) At **3 UTC**, examine the **direction and strength of wind along the cold front** and predict where Jonas will be at **9 UTC**. (2–3) Mark and check. (4–6) Repeat from 9 UTC to **15 UTC**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Two days:** Jonas moved **east-northeast**, about **2,000 km**, from Texas across the Southeast to the Atlantic just off **North Carolina**, carried by the **westerlies** (from the southwest).
- **6-hour steps:** The winds along the cold front blew from the **south and southwest**, so the low kept edging **north-northeast** up the coast, but **slowly** (only about 150 km every 6 hours) as it strengthened. That slow track kept heavy snow over the Mid-Atlantic and NYC for many hours.
- Your forecasts may be a bit off in distance. What matters is the **direction**: storms in the midlatitudes travel with the westerlies toward the **northeast**.
:::

# Evaluate: How Will Global Wind Patterns Be Affected by Rising Global Temperatures? {#sp-evaluate}

::: {.evaluate-box}
## 🌡️➡️🌬️ Will the Storm Highway Move?

Apply what you learned to predict **blizzards and hurricanes in the future**: analyze a climate model (a research article plus storm-track data) and decide **how confident** you are in it.
:::

## The research article {#sp-evaluate-article}

Your teacher provides an article. The student sample in the teacher guide uses ***"Will Global Warming Bring a Change in the Winds? Dust from the Deep Sea Provides a Clue"*** (Columbia Climate School, *State of the Planet*, January 2021), about a study published in *Nature* (Abell et al., 2021). Key points:

- **What they studied:** **dust** in deep-sea sediment cores from the **North Pacific**. Westerly winds carry dust from Asia out over the ocean, so the amount and location of dust is an **indirect tracer of the winds**.
- **When:** the **Pliocene**, about **3 to 5 million years ago**, when Earth was about **2–4 °C warmer** than today with roughly **the same CO₂ level as now**.
- **Finding:** during the warm Pliocene, the westerlies were **weaker** and located **closer to the poles** than during the colder periods that followed.
- **Claim about the future:** as Earth warms, the westerlies (and the storm tracks and rain belts they carry) will likely **keep shifting poleward** in both hemispheres.
- **Limits:** the study does **not** say exactly where it will rain more or less.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spQuiz("sp-article-quiz", "Check: The Article", [
  {q: "What MODEL are the researchers basing their claim on?",
   options: ["A balloon model", "The past: a warm period (the Pliocene) used as an analogue for the future, reconstructed from dust in ocean sediment cores", "This year's weather forecast", "A single storm track map"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "They use the Pliocene as a model of a warmer world. Dust records show where the westerlies were when Earth was 2–4 °C warmer."},
  {q: "What ASSUMPTION are they making?",
   options: ["That the winds of a past warm climate are a good guide to the winds of our future warm climate", "That dust never moves", "That Earth will cool", "That the Sun will get brighter"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Using the past as a model assumes the same causes lead to the same effects, even though continents, ice sheets and the speed of warming were not exactly the same 3 million years ago."}
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Evaluate guiding questions

1. What is the **claim** researchers are making about global wind patterns in the future?
2. What is the **model** they are basing their claims on?
3. What **assumptions** are the researchers making in order to use that model?
4. Based on the **diagram** in the article, how many degrees might the westerlies **move** if they followed the historic pattern?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. As global temperatures rise, the **westerlies will shift toward the poles** (north in our hemisphere) and weaken, moving storm tracks and rain belts with them.
2. A **past warm climate** (the Pliocene, 3–5 million years ago) reconstructed from **dust in North Pacific sediment cores**, compared with later cold periods.
3. That the **past is a good model** for the future: a world 2–4 °C warmer with similar CO₂ will have winds like the Pliocene's; that **dust reliably tracks the winds**; and that other differences (ice sheets, geography, the speed of today's warming) don't change the result much.
4. About **5°** of latitude north. That's the shift you'll test next.
:::

## What happens to storm tracks if the westerlies shift 5° north? {#sp-band-shift}

Your packet has **four winter storm track maps** (2014–15, 2016–17, 2018–19, 2019–20) with **5° latitude bands** from 25–30° N to 45–50° N. NYC is at about **40.7° N**, in the **40–45° N** band.

**How the model works:** count the storms that pass through each band. Then **shift every band's storms up one band** (5° north). The 40–45° N band then gets the storms that used to be in 35–40° N.

The counts below are **our rough counts from the packet maps** (a storm that crosses several bands counts in each). Counting is tricky, so **type in your own counts** if yours are different.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spBandNames = ["45–50° N", "40–45° N (NYC)", "35–40° N", "30–35° N", "25–30° N"]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
spBandEst = ({"2014–2015": [10, 17, 18, 13, 5], "2016–2017": [11, 18, 17, 6, 1], "2018–2019": [8, 17, 16, 9, 2], "2019–2020": [8, 13, 11, 5, 0]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof spSeason = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(spBandEst), {label: "Season:", value: "2018–2019"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const counts = spBandEst[spSeason].slice();
  const wrap = html`<div style="max-width:640px;margin:auto;"></div>`;
  const inputs = html`<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;margin-bottom:8px;"></div>`;
  const fields = counts.map((c, i) => {
    const box = html`<label style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;font-size:.8em;flex:1 1 100px;"><span>${spBandNames[i]}</span></label>`;
    const inp = html`<input type="number" min="0" max="40" value="${c}" style="min-height:40px;font-size:1em;padding:4px 8px;border-radius:8px;border:1.5px solid #94a3b8;background:#fff;color:#1e293b;width:100%;box-sizing:border-box;">`;
    box.appendChild(inp); inputs.appendChild(box); return inp;
  });
  const chartBox = html`<div></div>`, tableBox = html`<div class="sp-scroll"></div>`, msg = html`<div class="sp-readout"></div>`;
  const rank = arr => spBandNames.map((n, i) => ({n, v: arr[i]})).sort((a, b) => b.v - a.v);
  function update() {
    const now = fields.map(f => Math.max(0, +f.value || 0));
    const after = now.map((v, i) => i < 4 ? now[i + 1] : 0);
    const rows = [];
    spBandNames.forEach((n, i) => { rows.push({band: n, when: "Now", v: now[i]}); rows.push({band: n, when: "After 5° shift", v: after[i]}); });
    chartBox.innerHTML = "";
    chartBox.appendChild(Plot.plot({
      title: `Storms per latitude band, ${spSeason}`,
      width: Math.min(width, 640), height: 260, marginLeft: 110, marginRight: 30,
      x: {label: "Number of storms", grid: true, domain: [0, Math.max(20, d3.max(rows, d => d.v) + 2)]},
      y: {domain: ["Now", "After 5° shift"], axis: null},
      fy: {domain: spBandNames, label: null, axis: "left"},
      color: {domain: ["Now", "After 5° shift"], range: ["#3949ab", "#f59e0b"], legend: true},
      marks: [
        Plot.barX(rows, {fy: "band", y: "when", x: "v", fill: "when"}),
        Plot.text(rows, {fy: "band", y: "when", x: "v", text: "v", dx: 8, fontSize: 10, fill: "currentColor"})
      ]
    }));
    const r1 = rank(now), r2 = rank(after);
    const labels = ["Most", "Second Most", "Middle", "Second Least", "Least"];
    tableBox.innerHTML = `<table class="sp-table" style="min-width:460px;"><tr><th></th>${labels.map(l => `<th>${l}</th>`).join("")}</tr>
      <tr><td><b>Now</b></td>${r1.map(d => `<td>${d.n.replace(" (NYC)", "")} (${d.v})</td>`).join("")}</tr>
      <tr><td><b>After shift</b></td>${r2.map(d => `<td>${d.n.replace(" (NYC)", "")} (${d.v})</td>`).join("")}</tr></table>`;
    const a = now[1], b = after[1];
    const change = b > a ? `<b>more</b> storms (${a} → ${b})` : b < a ? `<b>fewer</b> storms (${a} → ${b})` : `the <b>same</b> number of storms (${a})`;
    msg.innerHTML = `📍 For NYC's band (40–45° N), this season's map predicts ${change} after the shift. The <b>45–50° N</b> band goes from ${now[0]} to ${after[0]}; the southern bands (25–35° N) go from ${now[3] + now[4]} to ${after[3] + after[4]}.`;
  }
  fields.forEach(f => f.addEventListener("input", update));
  update();
  wrap.appendChild(inputs); wrap.appendChild(chartBox); wrap.appendChild(tableBox); wrap.appendChild(msg);
  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const rows = Object.entries(spBandEst).map(([s, c]) => ({s, now: c[1], after: c[2]}));
  const tot = rows.reduce((a, r) => [a[0] + r.now, a[1] + r.after], [0, 0]);
  const long = rows.flatMap(r => [{s: r.s, when: "Now", v: r.now}, {s: r.s, when: "After 5° shift", v: r.after}]);
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    title: "NYC's band (40–45° N): all four seasons",
    subtitle: "Our rough counts from the packet maps",
    width: Math.min(width, 560), height: 230, marginBottom: 40,
    fx: {domain: Object.keys(spBandEst), label: null},
    x: {domain: ["Now", "After 5° shift"], axis: null}, y: {label: "Storms", grid: true},
    color: {domain: ["Now", "After 5° shift"], range: ["#3949ab", "#f59e0b"], legend: true},
    marks: [Plot.barY(long, {fx: "s", x: "when", y: "v", fill: "when"}), Plot.text(long, {fx: "s", x: "when", y: "v", text: "v", dy: -7, fontSize: 10, fill: "currentColor"}), Plot.ruleY([0])]
  });
  return html`<div style="max-width:560px;margin:auto;">${chart}<div class="sp-readout">Total over four seasons: <b>${tot[0]}</b> storms now vs. <b>${tot[1]}</b> after the shift (about ${Math.round((tot[1] - tot[0]) / tot[0] * 100)}%). One season goes up, three go down a little. The result is <b>small and not consistent</b>.</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: storm track maps and Analyze the data

For **each** of the four maps (2014–2015, 2016–2017, 2018–2019, 2019–2020):

1. **Rank** the latitude bands from **most** to **least** storms.
2. Imagine the storms all move **one band north**. **Re-rank** the bands.

**Analyze the data:**

1. Overall, what pattern do you see in which latitudes will receive **more** storms and which will receive **less**?
2. Look up the latitude of your school or home. How will **your area** be impacted if the westerlies move north 5°?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Rankings (our counts):** the busiest bands are **35–40° N and 40–45° N** in every season; the **25–30° N** band has the fewest. After the shift, **45–50° N** jumps to the top or near it, and **25–30° N** drops to almost zero.
- **Pattern:** **northern** latitudes (the northern US and southern Canada) would get **more** storms; **southern** latitudes (the southern US) would get **fewer**.
- **NYC (about 40.7° N):** NYC's band would get the storms that now cross **35–40° N**. On average that band has **slightly fewer** storms than NYC's band, so NYC might see **slightly fewer** winter storms, but one season (2014–15) shows the opposite. **The evidence is not clear-cut.** It's a small sample, and counting storms on these maps is imprecise. We would need **more data** to be confident.
:::

::: {.sp-note}
📝 **Note on the packet:** on the **2014–2015** map, the second band from the top is labeled "**30–45**". It should read **40–45** (the bands go 45–50, 40–45, 35–40, 30–35, 25–30).
:::

## 🔗 Connect to the Performance Task {#sp-connect-pt}

**Connect to the Performance Task: Paths of Severe Storms 5E** (Performance Task Organizer): *"Apply what you figured out from the Paths of Severe Storms 5E to respond to the prompt below. **Will the frequency of winter storms per year where you live increase, decrease, or stay the same as global temperatures increase in the future?**"*

- **Part 1:** Identify the **independent** and **dependent** variable.
- **Part 2:** Gather **evidence** from the investigation (What is the evidence? Which resource did it come from?).
- **Part 3:** Write an **argument from evidence**, with evidence and reasoning for your **claim** and for a **counterclaim**. Consider: historical winter storm frequency data, the conditions necessary for a winter storm to form, data from global climate models (such as projections of future temperatures), and the **reliability of the models** used to make predictions.

## 🔑 Sample argument (from the teacher guide's student work; write yours first!)

**Part 1:** IV = **global temperatures**; DV = **frequency of winter storms**.

**Part 2 evidence:** winds are predicted to shift north by about 5° (the article); on average fewer storms occur in the 5° band below NY than in NY's band (storm track maps); NY is at about 40° N, where global winds carry warm air from the south toward the north (Global Movement of Air Investigation, Explaining Global Wind Patterns); there is a low-precipitation band at 30° N (global precipitation diagram).

**Part 3 (paraphrased):** *As global temperatures increase, the frequency of blizzards in New York will **decrease**. New York is at about 40° N, where warm air moves north from southern latitudes because of global wind patterns, so as temperatures rise, the air moving north will be even warmer and less able to form snowstorms. Scientists predict the eastward-moving winds will shift 5° farther north. The low-precipitation band at 30° N could shift north too, pushing drier air toward New York. The storm track maps support this: on average, NY's band has more winter storms than the band below it, so if the winds shift north, NY would be in an area with fewer storms. **However**, this prediction is based on one idea about how winds could change. If rising temperatures cause polar air to disrupt other wind patterns, the impacts on NY may be different.*

What makes it strong: a clear **claim**, **several** pieces of evidence with sources, reasoning with **because/therefore**, and a **counterclaim** that questions the **model's reliability**. To reach Proficient, add **historical storm frequency data** and a **climate model temperature projection** (see [Unit 4](../unit4-climate-change/unit4-past-and-future.qmd)).
:::

**Still to figure out:** what specifically causes a **hurricane**, and will warming make hurricanes more frequent or more intense? That's the next chapter: [Hurricanes](unit5-hurricanes.qmd).

# Chapter Summary

| Key Concept | Details |
|---|---|
| **Uneven heating** | Same sunlight (1,361 W/m²) everywhere, but it's concentrated at the equator and spread out at the poles → warm tropics, cold poles |
| **Air masses** | Huge bodies of air that take on the temperature (latitude) and moisture (land/ocean) of where they form: cP, mP, cT, mT |
| **Why storms form over the US** | cP air from Canada and mT air from the Gulf of Mexico collide along the polar front |
| **Rising and sinking air** | Heated air → molecules spread out → less dense → rises → low pressure, clouds, rain. Cooled air → denser → sinks → high pressure, dry |
| **Pressure belts** | Low at 0° and 60°; high at 30° and the poles (Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells) |
| **Surface winds** | Flow from high to low pressure; bent by the Coriolis effect (right in NH, left in SH) → trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies |
| **Storm spin** | Air flowing into a low bends right → counterclockwise in the NH (clockwise in the SH) |
| **Storm paths** | Westerlies carry US winter storms SW → NE; trade winds carry hurricanes west, then the westerlies turn them northeast |
| **Future** | Warming may shift the westerlies ~5° poleward. For NYC (40.7° N) the storm-track evidence suggests slightly fewer winter storms, but it is uncertain |

```{ojs}
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        const all = card.querySelectorAll("button.sp-fq-opt");
        all.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; b.style.background = "#f8fafc"; b.style.color = "#475569"; });
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";btn.style.color="#276749";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color="#276749"; fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";btn.style.color="#9b2c2c";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          const c = all[qq.correct];
          c.style.borderColor="#48bb78";c.style.background="#f0fff4";c.style.color="#276749";c.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color="#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";fb.style.borderRadius="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    fb.className = "sp-fb";
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```
